title: The Endangered Species Act Reduces Housing - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: Max Tabarrok's Journal of Public Economics paper uses endangered species listings and de-listings as geographically bounded natural experiments and finds each listing cuts annual housing permits by 0.5 per thousand 1980 residents (~10% of the average place's flow), implying roughly 6.3 million missing US housing units over 1980-2024, about 4% of the 2025 housing stock. Crucially the ESA bites as hard on dense infill development, where the habitat tradeoff barely exists, as on exurban greenfield sprawl.

insights.claim: Endangered species listings function as geographically bounded regulatory natural experiments because compliance costs and liability risk bind only where the listed species lives, with the US list growing from 82 listings in 1970 to nearly 1500 today plus occasional de-listings that run the treatment in reverse.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: A clean identification design for pricing US land-use regulation risk; the same treatment/control logic can be reused to value other geographically scoped environmental rules against homebuilder land banks.
insights.quote: the ESA creates many natural experiments, places where it binds and nearby places where it doesn’t
insights.locator: Max Tabarrok’s paper on the Endangered Species Act

insights.claim: After the Northern Long Eared Bat was added to the endangered species list, annual housing permits per 1000 1980 population fell in potential bat-habitat areas relative to nearby control areas, and when the Peregrine falcon was de-listed, previously suppressed habitat areas caught up to their controls.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: The effect is symmetric in both directions, so de-regulatory ESA relief should show up as a measurable permit uplift rather than a one-way ratchet — a real catalyst for homebuilders in habitat-heavy geographies.
insights.quote: After the bat was put on the endangered species list, the number of new housing permits declined in areas where bats might live relative to control areas.
insights.locator: The bottom left panel measures annual housing permits

insights.claim: The paper extends its permit-based specification to satellite land-use data from the National Land Cover Database, which classifies 30-square-meter pixels into fifteen land use groups annually back to 1985, to measure the hazard rate of greenfield conversion as non-developed pixels flow into developed classes.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Satellite land-cover panels are becoming a cheap independent check on permit statistics — a data source worth tracking for real-time reads on construction activity and land conversion.
insights.quote: They classify 30-square-meter pixels into one of fifteen land use groups, including four levels of development, three types of forest, and two types of wetland.
insights.locator: The NLCD is a set of satellite images

insights.claim: Each additional endangered species listing reduces annual housing permit flows by 0.5 permits per thousand 1980 residents, roughly 10% of the average place's permit flow.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Quantifies a single-species listing as a ~10% hit to local permitting — a concrete regulatory-risk haircut to apply to land holdings in newly listed habitat.

insights.claim: Accounting for spillovers and diminishing costs, the aggregate effect of the Endangered Species Act has been to reduce the US national housing stock by roughly 6.3 million missing units over 1980-2024, about 4% of the 2025 housing stock.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Puts a single federal environmental statute on the same order of magnitude as the widely cited national housing shortage, making ESA reform a genuine supply lever for shelter inflation.
insights.quote: roughly 6.3 million missing units over 1980–2024, about 4% of the 2025 housing stock
insights.locator: Accounting for spillovers and diminishing costs

themes.theme: Infill bites hardest — the policy arbitrage

insights.claim: The most urbanized 15% of US places account for 90% of total permit flows while the highest-value endangered species habitat lies well outside those developed areas, so the ESA restricts dense infill development about as much as it restricts greenfield development in exurban sprawl.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: The ESA's biggest housing cost is being paid where it buys no habitat protection at all — the strongest analytic case yet that environmental and housing lobbies are fighting over a false tradeoff.

insights.claim: On the intensive margin, new development typically replaces existing buildings or fills space in already-dense areas that could not host endangered species regardless, so relaxing the ESA there is potentially positive sum because it substitutes for less dense greenfield building.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Frames a reform that both YIMBYs and environmentalists can sign — the politically feasible version of ESA relief, and the one to watch in legislative text.
insights.quote: On the intensive margin, the tradeoff with species protection does not bind, and may even be positive sum as it substitutes for less dense greenfield development.
insights.locator: …at the intensive margin of housing production

insights.claim: Narrowing the Endangered Species Act's legal bite in already-built-up areas would shift permit flows toward dense, energy- and land-efficient cities in California and on the East Coast at the expense of sprawling Sun Belt suburbs.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: A geographic rotation trade inside homebuilding and construction materials: coastal urban infill volumes up, Sun Belt land-development volumes relatively down.
insights.quote: may increase permit flows in dense, energy- and land-efficient cities in California and on the East Coast at the expense of sprawling suburbs in the Sun Belt
insights.locator: Relaxing the legal mechanism of the Endangered Species Act

insights.claim: The Trump administration is actively trying to limit the Endangered Species Act and multiple lawsuits have already been filed, making the timing of quantified ESA-versus-housing evidence unusually consequential.
insights.speaker: Alex Tabarrok
insights.so_what: Live regulatory and litigation catalyst — the court outcomes set whether the 6.3 million-unit supply constraint starts loosening or is locked in.
insights.quote: The Trump administration is trying to limit the ESA, multiple lawsuits have already been filed.
